factProposals.value: A management company does not own rows in the public `hospitals` table -- it manages a subset of them via a new company_hospitals join table. The public CMS data (hospitals, cost_report_years, early_warning_flags) stays public-read regardless of company scoping; only the private operator-uploaded tables (hospital_monthly_metrics, export_conversions, slipping_hospital_alerts) are scoped by company.

anon and authenticated Postgres roles already hold blanket ALL-privilege grants (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) on every table in this schema via Supabase's schema-level default -- row-level security is the only mechanism restricting what those roles can actually see or change, confirmed by querying information_schema.role_table_grants directly rather than assumed.
factProposals.evidence: PROGRESS.md STORY-006 entry, Verification section (live grant query)

factProposals.value: auth.uid() in this Supabase instance reads the request.jwt.claim.sub Postgres session setting (confirmed via pg_get_functiondef, not assumed from generic Supabase docs), and the DATABASE_URL connection's role (postgres) has rolbypassrls=true -- it bypasses RLS entirely as the table owner, which is why the Python pipeline's existing writes were never subject to RLS and needed no changes for this story.

RLS policies that reference other tables in their USING clause are themselves subject to those other tables' RLS, evaluated under the querying role's own privileges, not the table owner's. A policy chain (hospital_monthly_metrics -> company_hospitals -> company_members) breaks silently (always zero rows, for every user) unless every table in the chain has its own policy permitting at least the legitimate self-referential read.
factProposals.evidence: pipeline/schema.sql (company_members' 'see own membership' policy, required for company_hospitals' and companies' own policies to resolve at all)

factProposals.value: company_members.user_id is a bare uuid, not foreign-keyed to auth.users(id) -- no real Supabase Auth sign-up/sign-in flow exists yet in this repo, so there are no real users to reference. This will need revisiting once a real auth flow exists.

decisions.statement: Built .colaberry's literal 3 acceptance criteria (real schema + real RLS + a real cross-company isolation test) but deliberately did not build a sign-in UI in this story, even though .hospulse's more detailed blueprint for the same requirement includes one.
decisions.rationale: .colaberry's criteria talk about 'accessing data', not a login form. No story in the 13-story plan is explicitly 'build the sign-in screen'. Building a full auth UI now risks being redone once STORY-007/008 (briefings, email) clarify what operator-facing pages actually need. Raised with the user and confirmed before building.

decisions.statement: Modeled company-to-hospital assignment as a new company_hospitals join table rather than adding a company_id column directly to the private data tables (hospital_monthly_metrics, export_conversions, slipping_hospital_alerts).
decisions.rationale: A company manages a hospital, it doesn't own the private data rows directly -- the join lets scoping work entirely through provider_ccn, so no changes were needed to the upload path (STORY-005) or the normalizer's write logic to attribute a company at write time.
decisions.evidence: pipeline/schema.sql (company_hospitals table, and the three 'company scoped read' policies that join through it)

decisions.statement: Added a nullable provider_ccn column to export_conversions rather than leaving its audit rows permanently unscoped by any company.
decisions.rationale: export_conversions had no hospital reference at all before this story -- without one, its rows could never be attributed to any company, leaving the upload audit trail either fully public or fully inaccessible to the operator who created it. A needs_mapping conversion genuinely has no identifiable hospital (the format was never recognized), so it correctly stays NULL rather than guessing.

decisions.statement: Wrote a real, permanent, opt-in-only integration test (pipeline/test_row_level_security.py) that exercises actual Postgres RLS via session-level JWT claim simulation, rather than treating the live verification as a one-off manual script.
decisions.rationale: This is the Trust criterion for a security feature, and 'data leakage' is an explicit failure path to prevent -- a security boundary this important deserves a permanent, re-runnable regression test using the real mechanism, not just a manual proof that gets discarded. Kept out of the default pytest pipeline/ sweep (skipped unless RUN_RLS_INTEGRATION_TESTS=1 is set) per this project's own rule that integration tests must never run automatically against production.
decisions.evidence: pipeline/test_row_level_security.py module docstring; confirmed skipped by default in the full pipeline/ suite

limitations.statement: No real Supabase Auth sign-up/sign-in flow exists yet, so company_members.user_id values used in testing are synthetic UUIDs, not real authenticated users. The RLS mechanism itself is proven correct; it has not been exercised through an actual browser sign-in session.
limitations.evidence: pipeline/test_row_level_security.py (uses uuid.uuid4() for user_a/user_b/stranger, not real auth.users rows)

limitations.statement: No UI exists yet for assigning hospitals to companies or managing company membership -- companies, company_members, and company_hospitals rows can currently only be created via direct database access (as this story's own test does), not through any application interface.
limitations.evidence: No frontend code references these tables yet -- grep of frontend/src/ confirms zero usages

demonstrationEvidence.ref: pipeline/test_export_normalizer.py (+3 tests: export_conversions.provider_ccn attribution for ok/needs_mapping/failed outcomes)
